operational_lifetime: About 21 hours 36 minutes as a crewed base on the surface (20–21 July 1969)
original_purpose: The descent stage carried Armstrong and Aldrin from lunar orbit to the surface. It held the descent engine, the landing gear, most of the consumables and the modular equipment stowage bay that carried the EASEP experiments and the commemorative plaque. Once on the ground it became the launch platform for the ascent stage.
mission_story: Eagle separated from the command module Columbia on 20 July 1969 and made a powered descent that ended at 20:17:40 UTC in Mare Tranquillitatis. The intended landing point was several kilometres downrange of the actual touchdown, so the crew flew a manual redesignation to a smoother area and landed with roughly 25 seconds of hovering fuel remaining. Armstrong and Aldrin spent about 21 hours on the surface, including a 2 hour 31 minute moonwalk, before the ascent stage fired and returned them to Columbia.
operational_history: The descent stage had no independent function after separation: its job was to get the crew down intact and to serve as a stable, level platform for the ascent stage's launch. Its structure held the ladder, the porch, the plaque, the flag assembly and the stowage bay from which the Early Apollo Scientific Experiments Package was unpacked.

scientific_contribution.title: A fixed, surveyed platform for the first lunar seismometer
scientific_contribution.text: Because the descent stage's position was precisely tracked, the experiment package deployed 16.8 m from it could be located to metres — the reference point from which the Apollo 11 seismic station was surveyed.

scientific_contribution.title: The reference landmark of Tranquility Base
scientific_contribution.text: Every sample, photograph and experiment of the mission is positioned relative to the descent stage, which is why the site remains one of the best-surveyed places on the Moon.

final_status: The descent stage remains at Tranquility Base, where it has been imaged from lunar orbit by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter since 2009. It is the largest single piece of hardware left by Apollo 11.
why_it_matters: Eagle's descent stage is the physical marker of the first crewed landing on another world — the object around which the archaeological site of Tranquility Base is defined.

facts.label: Mass left behind
facts.value: Descent stage of the 15.1 t Lunar Module

facts.label: Still there?
facts.value: Yes — imaged from orbit by LRO

short_name: Apollo 11 Early Apollo Scientific Experiments Package (EASEP)
operational_lifetime: Seismometer: 21 days (21 July – 27 August 1969). Retroreflector: still in use.
original_purpose: A simplified, solar-powered experiment package for a test-flight landing: a passive seismometer to listen for moonquakes and meteoroid impacts, and a laser ranging retroreflector to measure the Earth–Moon distance.
mission_story: Aldrin unpacked the two EASEP elements from the descent stage's storage bay and set them up a short walk from Eagle. The package was deliberately small — Apollo 11 was a demonstration flight, and the full ALSEP stations came later — but it produced the first seismic record from another world.
operational_history: The seismometer was activated on 21 July 1969 and returned data for 21 days. It recorded the astronauts' own footsteps and equipment handling, the impact of discarded hardware, and a small number of natural events. Commanding became impossible on 27 August 1969 and the experiment was terminated. Its solar cells limited it to lunar day, and internal temperatures ran about 28 °C hotter than designed.

scientific_contribution.title: The first seismic record from another world
scientific_contribution.text: The passive seismometer proved that lunar seismic exploration was feasible and that natural moonquakes and meteoroid impacts could be detected — the result that justified the four-station Apollo network.

scientific_contribution.title: A retroreflector that still measures the Moon
scientific_contribution.text: The laser ranging retroreflector is a passive array of corner-cube prisms. Ranging stations on Earth still bounce laser pulses off it today, measuring the Earth–Moon distance to centimetres and testing gravitational physics.

final_status: The seismometer is inert at Tranquility Base. The retroreflector has no electronics, no power supply and no moving parts, and remains functional and in regular use by international laser ranging stations.
why_it_matters: It is the clearest example in this archive of hardware that outlived its mission: one half failed within three weeks, the other half has now been returning data for more than five decades.

facts.label: Experiments
facts.value: Passive Seismic Experiment Package + Laser Ranging Retroreflector

timeline.detail: Seismometer activated at 04:41 UTC; first seismic data returned.

timeline.label: Seismometer fails

timeline.label: Retroreflector keeps working
timeline.detail: Passive optics need no power — laser ranging continues.

operational_lifetime: 14 days of surface operations (20 April – 4 May 1967); 31 months on the Moon before the Apollo 12 visit
original_purpose: A robotic soft-lander built to prove that the lunar surface could carry a spacecraft, to return close-up television images of the terrain and to measure the soil's mechanical properties before astronauts attempted a landing.
mission_story: Surveyor 3 launched on 17 April 1967 and landed on 20 April after a descent in which radar returns from highly reflective rocks confused the guidance; the engine cut off late, and the spacecraft bounced twice before settling in a crater in southeastern Oceanus Procellarum. It transmitted 6,326 television pictures and dug into the soil with a mechanical scoop.
operational_history: The lander operated through the first lunar day. Controllers lost contact on 4 May 1967, two days after lunar nightfall, and it could not be revived at the next sunrise. Two and a half years later, on 19 November 1969, the crew of Apollo 12 landed the lunar module Intrepid about 155–180 m away and walked over to it during the second moonwalk — the only time people have visited a spacecraft on another world.

scientific_contribution.title: Soil mechanics that cleared Apollo to land
scientific_contribution.text: The scoop's bearing tests showed the surface soil behaved like wet sand — firm enough to support a lander. That measurement directly informed the Apollo landing design.

scientific_contribution.title: Returned hardware: 31 months of exposure, measured
scientific_contribution.text: Apollo 12 astronauts cut away the television camera, the soil scoop, structural tubing and cable, and brought them home. Laboratory analysis of those parts gave engineers the first direct data on how coatings, seals and electronics age in vacuum, radiation and repeated thermal cycling.

final_status: Surveyor 3 remains in its crater, minus the components removed by Apollo 12. The returned television camera is in the collection of the National Air and Space Museum; part of the scoop is displayed at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory.
why_it_matters: It is the only probe on another world that humans have walked up to, inspected and taken pieces of — a robotic precursor that became an archaeological site and a materials-science experiment at the same time.

operational_lifetime: Six and a half years (5 February 1971 – 30 September 1977)
original_purpose: A nuclear-powered geophysics station: a passive seismometer, an active seismic experiment that fired small explosive charges into the ground, a suprathermal ion detector, a cold-cathode ion gauge and a charged-particle experiment.
mission_story: Shepard and Mitchell pulled the two ALSEP sub-packages from the side of the Antares descent stage, loaded them on a hand-pulled cart and set the station up about 180 m west of the lunar module in the Fra Mauro highlands — the rugged ejecta blanket thrown out by the impact that formed Mare Imbrium.
operational_history: The station was activated on 5 February 1971 and ran on a radioisotope thermoelectric generator, so unlike Apollo 11's solar-powered package it worked through the lunar night. Mitchell spent 48 minutes firing 21 thumper charges by hand and the mortar package later launched four grenades on command, all recorded by three geophones. Operations ended when NASA shut down the whole ALSEP network on 30 September 1977 for budget reasons, not because the hardware had failed.

scientific_contribution.title: The layered structure of the lunar crust
scientific_contribution.text: The active seismic experiment measured seismic wave speeds to depths of roughly 300 m, resolving the regolith and the fractured bedrock beneath Fra Mauro — a direct measurement of the Moon's upper crust.

scientific_contribution.title: One corner of the Apollo seismic network
scientific_contribution.text: With stations at Apollo 12, 14, 15 and 16, the network could locate moonquake sources and later constrain the size of the lunar core. Apollo 14's seismometer was the most sensitive of the four.

scientific_contribution.title: Charged particles at the lunar surface
scientific_contribution.text: The charged-particle experiment measured solar protons and electrons reaching the ground, while the suprathermal ion detector and cold-cathode gauge characterised the thin lunar plasma and neutral atmosphere.

final_status: The ALSEP station is inert at Fra Mauro, its transmitter silent since 30 September 1977. The hardware — central station, geophones, mortar package, antennas — is still on the surface.
why_it_matters: It is a case of equipment switched off rather than worn out: the station was working when the programme ended, which is why its records remain a benchmark for lunar seismology.

facts.value: Passive seismic, active seismic, suprathermal ion detector, cold-cathode gauge, charged particles

operational_lifetime: Three days of driving; three EVAs totalling 18 h 13 min on the surface
original_purpose: The first crewed surface vehicle on another world: a battery-powered, four-wheel-drive rover built to extend the astronauts' geological reach from a few hundred metres to tens of kilometres, carrying two people, tools and samples.
mission_story: Falcon landed at Hadley-Apennine on 30 July 1971, at the foot of the Apennine mountains beside Hadley Rille. The rover unfolded from the side of the descent stage during the first moonwalk; deployment gave trouble at first, and the crew had to work through it before driving to Elbow Crater.
operational_history: Over three EVAs the rover carried Scott and Irwin 27.9 km, reaching the base of Hadley Delta, the edge of Hadley Rille and the Apennine front. On the last EVA Scott drove it a short distance past the lunar module and parked it about 160 m east so that its television camera could watch the ascent stage lift off. It has not moved since.

scientific_contribution.title: Reach equals rock record
scientific_contribution.text: By multiplying the area the crew could sample, the rover made the Apollo 15 haul possible: about 77 kg of samples spanning mare basalt, highland anorthosite and the layered deposits of Hadley Rille.

scientific_contribution.title: Proof that mobility changes mission design
scientific_contribution.text: The rover's navigation system, its wire-mesh wheels and its thermal design set the template for every later surface vehicle, including the Mars rovers.

scientific_contribution.title: The Genesis Rock
scientific_contribution.text: At Spur Crater on the second EVA the crew collected sample 15415, an anorthosite later dated to roughly four billion years — a piece of the Moon's original highland crust.

final_status: The rover sits where Scott parked it in August 1971, about 160 m east of the Falcon descent stage. Its tracks and its shadow are visible in Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter images.
why_it_matters: It is the vehicle that turned a landing site into a region — and the first machine to carry humans across the surface of another world.

facts.value: About 160 m east of the lunar module

operational_lifetime: Operated during the three-day surface stay (21–23 April 1972)
original_purpose: A tripod-mounted, 75 mm f/1.0 electronographic Schmidt camera built to image the sky and the Earth in far-ultraviolet light from a place with no atmosphere to block it.
mission_story: Apollo 16 landed in the Descartes highlands on 20 April 1972. John Young carried the 22 kg instrument out of Orion, set it on its tripod in the shadow of the lunar module so that it would stay cold and free of stray sunlight, and re-aimed it by hand at targets chosen by the science team on Earth.
operational_history: The camera worked in two modes — direct imaging and spectroscopy — and the crew re-pointed it at the Earth, at auroral and airglow regions, at star fields, nebulae and the Large Magellanic Cloud. During the third EVA the film cartridge was removed and returned to Earth; the telescope itself was left standing on the surface.

scientific_contribution.title: The first observatory on another world
scientific_contribution.text: The experiment returned 178 frames of far-ultraviolet data — the first astronomical observations made from the surface of a planetary body other than Earth.

scientific_contribution.title: The shape of Earth's hydrogen geocorona
scientific_contribution.text: Images and spectra below 1600 Å mapped atomic hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen emissions around the Earth, including the extended geocorona and a pronounced sunward/antisunward asymmetry.

scientific_contribution.title: Aurorae and the tropical airglow belt
scientific_contribution.text: The camera produced the first ultraviolet images of Earth's auroral zones and the equatorial airglow belt, showing structure that had never been seen pictorially.

final_status: The camera remains on the Moon in the Descartes highlands, in the shadow of the Orion descent stage, with its film cartridge long since returned to Earth.
why_it_matters: It is the first and so far only astronomical observatory on the surface of another world — and the reason later missions treat the Moon as a platform for instruments rather than only as a destination.

facts.label: Principal investigator
facts.value: George R. Carruthers, US Naval Research Laboratory

facts.label: Present state
facts.value: Left on the Moon; film returned to Earth

operational_lifetime: Three EVAs over three days (11–14 December 1972)
original_purpose: The third flight rover: the vehicle that would let the last Apollo crew work across the widest geological range of the programme, from the valley floor to the bases of the North and South Massifs.
mission_story: Cernan and Schmitt landed in the Taurus-Littrow valley on 11 December 1972, a deep valley cut into the lunar highlands and partly filled with mare basalt. The rover let them sample both: ancient highland material tumbled down from the massifs and younger volcanic deposits on the valley floor.
operational_history: Across three EVAs the crew drove roughly 35.7 km by the rover's odometer, reaching nine geological stations and deploying explosive packages for a seismic profiling experiment. On the last EVA they stopped at Shorty crater, where Schmitt spotted orange soil — tiny beads of volcanic glass that record an explosive eruption. The rover was parked near the lunar module before the crew left; it is the last vehicle humans have driven on another world.

scientific_contribution.title: Orange glass and the Moon's volcanic past
scientific_contribution.text: The orange soil at Shorty crater turned out to be pyroclastic glass beads, evidence of fire-fountain eruptions around 3.5 billion years ago — a sample type the earlier missions had not found.

scientific_contribution.title: A cross-section of the highlands
scientific_contribution.text: Material sampled at the base of the South Massif included a bright landslide deposit, giving the mission access to deep highland crust without climbing it. Apollo 17 returned 110.5 kg of samples, the largest haul of the programme.

scientific_contribution.title: Active seismic profiling of a valley
scientific_contribution.text: The lunar seismic profiling experiment detonated eight explosive packages along the valley floor and recorded the returns, mapping the structure of the regolith and the buried valley floor.

final_status: The rover is parked near the Apollo 17 lunar module at Taurus-Littrow, where its tracks and its shadow appear in Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter imagery. The mission's descent stage, ALSEP and the crew's footprints are all within a few hundred metres.
why_it_matters: It is the most travelled crewed vehicle off Earth and the last one: no human has driven on the Moon since December 1972.

facts.label: Notable find
facts.value: Orange pyroclastic glass at Shorty crater

short_name: Mars Pathfinder Lander (Carl Sagan Memorial Station)
operational_lifetime: 83 sols (4 July – 27 September 1997), against a 30-sol design life
original_purpose: A technology demonstration that landed with airbags rather than retro-rockets, and a science station carrying a stereo imager on a mast and a meteorology package.
mission_story: Pathfinder hit the Martian atmosphere at about 7.3 km/s on 4 July 1997, was slowed by a heat shield and parachute, and then dropped inside a cocoon of airbags that bounced it some fifteen times across Ares Vallis before it came to rest. The petals opened, the lander stood itself upright, and a small rover rolled down a ramp two days later.
operational_history: The lander's imager and meteorology package ran for three months, returning panoramas of a boulder-strewn flood plain and a continuous weather record. It also relayed every command and image for the rover. Contact was lost on 27 September 1997 — a final carrier signal with no data was heard on 7 October — and the team concluded that a depleted battery and falling temperatures had ended the mission. Recovery attempts continued until March 1998.

scientific_contribution.title: Daily weather on another planet
scientific_contribution.text: The atmosphere structure and meteorology package recorded pressure, temperature and wind through the whole mission, including the passage of dust devils — vortices detected as sharp pressure dips.

scientific_contribution.title: A flood plain, read from the ground
scientific_contribution.text: The lander's images and the rover's spectrometer showed rounded pebbles and andesitic rocks consistent with material deposited and reworked by catastrophic flooding.

scientific_contribution.title: The landing system that made cheap Mars missions possible
scientific_contribution.text: Airbag entry, descent and landing, and the rover-relay architecture, became the basis for later low-cost Mars landers.

final_status: The lander is inactive in Ares Vallis. Nothing has returned to the site, but the hardware and its deflated airbags remain where the mission ended.
why_it_matters: Pathfinder reopened Mars for small, frequent missions and carried the first rover to another planet — the lander is the anchor point for both stories.

timeline.detail: Pathfinder leaves Earth on a Delta II.

timeline.label: Airbag landing in Ares Vallis

name: Mars Pathfinder Lander (Carl Sagan Memorial Station)

operational_lifetime: 83 sols — about twelve times its seven-sol design life
original_purpose: A 11.5 kg six-wheeled technology demonstrator: could a small, cheap rover be driven on Mars from Earth, with a ten-minute round-trip light time forcing it to look after itself?
mission_story: Sojourner stood up to its full 30 cm height on the night of 5 July 1997 and rolled down the lander's rear ramp at 05:37 UTC on 6 July. It then circled the lander in a clockwise direction, approaching rocks that the science team picked from the lander's images.
operational_history: The rover carried an alpha proton X-ray spectrometer, a colour camera at the rear and two black-and-white cameras at the front. It measured the composition of rocks and soils at a series of targets, took more than 550 images and demonstrated obstacle avoidance and autonomous hazard detection. When the lander fell silent in September 1997 the rover was still working; its last measured target was a rock nicknamed Chimp.

scientific_contribution.title: Rock chemistry at a flood plain
scientific_contribution.text: The alpha proton X-ray spectrometer showed that the rocks around the lander were silica-rich andesites rather than the expected basalts, evidence that the material had been through more complex geological processing.

scientific_contribution.title: Microrovers become practical
scientific_contribution.text: Sojourner proved that a rover small enough to be carried by a lander could navigate, survive and do real science — the direct ancestor of every subsequent Mars rover.

final_status: The rover's final position is not known. When the lander stopped relaying, Sojourner was following stored commands; engineers expected it to circle the lander or stand still and wait. It is somewhere within a few tens of metres of the lander in Ares Vallis.
why_it_matters: It is the machine that turned rovers from a speculative idea into a standard instrument of planetary exploration.

timeline.detail: The rover rides the lander down inside its airbag cocoon.

timeline.label: Rolls onto the surface

name: Sojourner Rover

operational_lifetime: 2,210 sols (6 years 2 months), against a 90-sol design life
original_purpose: One of a pair of golf-cart-sized geological rovers sent to test whether Mars had ever been wet enough to support life, using a suite of cameras and spectrometers on a rock-abrasion tool.
mission_story: Spirit landed inside Gusev crater on 4 January 2004 — a site chosen because it looked like an ancient lake basin. When the crater floor turned out to be a plain of volcanic rock, the team drove 3 km to the Columbia Hills, where the rover found the layered, altered rocks that the mission had been sent to look for.
operational_history: Spirit climbed Husband Hill, descended to the volcanic plateau called Home Plate, and survived three Martian winters and two major dust storms. In May 2009 it broke through a crust into soft soil on the west side of Home Plate at a spot now called Troy and became permanently embedded. It was reclassified as a stationary science platform, and its last contact was on sol 2210, 22 March 2010. Recovery attempts ended in 2011.

scientific_contribution.title: Hot springs on early Mars
scientific_contribution.text: Near Home Plate the rover found nearly pure silica deposits, best explained by hydrothermal fluids — water circulating through volcanic rock — which is one of the strongest habitability indicators found by either MER rover.

scientific_contribution.title: Water-altered rocks in the Columbia Hills
scientific_contribution.text: Sulphate-rich outcrops and altered basalts in the hills recorded multiple episodes of liquid water interacting with rock early in Martian history.

scientific_contribution.title: Dust devils as cleaning events
scientific_contribution.text: Spirit's power output jumped after dust devils passed over the arrays, a discovery that changed how solar-powered Mars missions are designed and operated.

final_status: Spirit is silent and embedded at Troy on the western side of Home Plate. The rover's last commanded state was a low-power hibernation from which it never woke; the most probable cause is cold damage to its survival heaters and batteries.
why_it_matters: Spirit turned a three-month geology experiment into a six-year expedition, and its final resting place is a monument to how much a mission can outlive its plan.

timeline.label: Landing in Gusev crater
timeline.detail: Spirit arrives inside an airbag cocoon.

timeline.label: Husband Hill summit

name: Spirit Rover (MER-A)

operational_lifetime: 5,111 sols (14 years 5 months), against a 90-sol design life
original_purpose: Spirit's twin, sent to the Meridiani Planum because orbital spectroscopy had detected coarse-grained haematite there — a mineral that on Earth usually forms in water.
mission_story: Opportunity landed on 25 January 2004 and came to rest inside a small crater barely 22 m across. Within weeks it found what it had been sent for: millimetre-scale haematite concretions, nicknamed blueberries, embedded in layered sedimentary rock. The site had once been a shallow, salty body of water.
operational_history: The rover went on to spend fourteen years crossing Meridiani Planum, descending into Victoria crater and then driving roughly 21 km to the 22 km-wide Endeavour crater, which it reached in August 2011. In 2018 it was working down a gully on the western rim called Perseverance Valley when a planet-wide dust storm cut its power. Its last transmission was on 10 June 2018; NASA declared the mission over on 13 February 2019.

scientific_contribution.title: Acidic, salty water once stood here
scientific_contribution.text: The sedimentary rocks at Meridiani — haematite concretions, sulphate-rich sandstones and cross-bedding — record shallow acidic water that evaporated repeatedly, one of the clearest ancient aqueous environments found on Mars.

scientific_contribution.title: Gypsum veins at Endeavour
scientific_contribution.text: On the rim of Endeavour crater the rover found calcium sulphate veins deposited by water flowing through fractures, showing that water moved through the crust long after the lakebeds formed.

scientific_contribution.title: The long traverse
scientific_contribution.text: Opportunity's 45.16 km set the off-world driving record and stood until NASA's Perseverance rover passed it in October 2026.

final_status: Opportunity is silent in Perseverance Valley on the western rim of Endeavour crater. More than a thousand recovery commands went unanswered; the rover is presumed to have suffered either a catastrophic failure or a fatal coating of dust on its solar arrays.
why_it_matters: It is the longest-lived surface mission in the archive and the one that converted 'was Mars ever habitable?' from a hypothesis into a field observation.

name: Opportunity Rover (MER-B)

operational_lifetime: Four years and one month (26 November 2018 – 15 December 2022 last contact)
original_purpose: A geophysics station rather than a geology mission: a seismometer, a heat-flow probe and a radio experiment built to measure the interior of Mars — its crust, mantle and core — for the first time.
mission_story: InSight landed in western Elysium Planitia on 26 November 2018, a deliberately boring patch of flat ground chosen for safety rather than scenery. Its instruments were placed on the surface by a robotic arm, not by astronauts, over the following weeks — the first time a seismometer had been deployed directly onto another planet.
operational_history: The seismometer ran from early 2019 until the end. The heat probe, designed to hammer itself 5 m into the ground, could not get traction in the soil and stopped at about 40 cm, a well-documented instrument failure. Dust accumulating on the solar arrays steadily reduced power until the lander entered a low-power mode and, on 15 December 2022, fell silent. NASA declared the mission over on 21 December 2022.

scientific_contribution.title: 1,319 marsquakes and a map of the interior
scientific_contribution.text: SEIS detected more than 1,300 seismic events, including meteoroid impacts. The data constrained the thickness of the Martian crust, the structure of the mantle and the size of a liquid core — the first seismic model of another planet since Apollo.

scientific_contribution.title: Weather and magnetic environment
scientific_contribution.text: The lander's pressure, wind and temperature sensors produced a multi-year surface weather record, and its magnetometer measured the remnants of Mars's extinct magnetic dynamo in the rocks beneath it.

scientific_contribution.title: Impacts as a clock
scientific_contribution.text: Seismic signals from meteoroid impacts, including a large event that exposed boulder-sized chunks of ice, gave a new way to date surfaces and to study the crust's ice content.

final_status: The lander is inactive on the surface of Elysium Planitia, its solar panels covered in dust. Its seismometer was the last instrument still powered when the mission ended.
why_it_matters: InSight is the direct descendant of the Apollo seismometers in this archive: the same technique, applied to a whole planet, half a century later.

facts.label: Instruments
facts.value: SEIS seismometer, HP³ heat probe, RISE radio experiment, weather package

name: InSight Lander

short_name: Viking 1 Lander (Thomas A. Mutch Memorial Station)
operational_lifetime: Six years four months (2,245 sols), against a 90-sol primary mission
original_purpose: The first successful Mars lander: to image the surface, analyse the atmosphere and soil, monitor the weather, and run three biology experiments designed to look for signs of microbial life.
mission_story: Viking 1 arrived at Mars on 19 June 1976 and spent a month in orbit while its cameras looked for a safe landing site; the original target was rejected as too rough. The lander separated on 20 July 1976 and touched down on the western slopes of Chryse Planitia, sending back the first photograph ever taken from the surface of Mars within minutes.
operational_history: The primary mission lasted 90 sols. The lander then kept working for another six years as a weather station — daily, then weekly reports — long after the biology and imaging programmes had ended. It was renamed the Thomas A. Mutch Memorial Station in 1982. On 11 November 1982 a faulty command uploaded from Earth interrupted communications, and the lander never responded again.

scientific_contribution.title: The first direct test for life on Mars
scientific_contribution.text: The labelled-release experiment produced a positive result, but the gas chromatograph–mass spectrometer found no organic molecules at the landing sites, and the consensus interpretation is that the signal came from reactive soil chemistry rather than biology. The result defined the terms of the habitability debate for the next two decades.

scientific_contribution.title: A six-year Martian weather record
scientific_contribution.text: The lander's meteorology package measured pressure, temperature and wind for more than six years, including seasonal cycles and dust storms — still one of the longest continuous surface climate series for Mars.

scientific_contribution.title: Hardware that outlived its design by decades
scientific_contribution.text: The lander operated for 2,245 sols on hardware designed for 90, an engineering case study in long-duration surface operations.

final_status: The lander is inactive on the surface of Chryse Planitia. Contact was never regained and the mission was formally concluded in 1983.
why_it_matters: It is the oldest human-made object still sitting on Mars, and the mission that established what a Mars lander can do — including how long one can keep working.

timeline.detail: Viking 1 leaves Earth on a Titan-Centaur.
